title: Sharing the Road
summary: How to drive safely around pedestrians, bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks, school buses, trains, emergency vehicles, work crews and slow farm traffic.

items: Watch especially carefully for pedestrians near schools, parks, playgrounds and bus stops.
Children may run into the street without looking, often from between parked cars. Slow down when they are near the road.
Children on bicycles are unpredictable. Expect them to swerve or ride into the street without looking.
Before you back out of a driveway, check behind your car for small children, and keep checking while you back up.
Where there is no sidewalk, pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road, facing oncoming traffic.
A pedestrian using a white cane or a guide dog is blind or visually impaired. Stop and give them the right-of-way, and do not honk; it can confuse them.

blocks.text: Obey a school crossing guard just as you would a police officer. If the guard holds up a STOP sign, stop, even if your light is green.
Bicyclists on the road have the same rights and responsibilities as other drivers. They must ride in the same direction as traffic, usually near the right side of the lane or in a bike lane.

items: A bicyclist may legally move left, away from the edge, to avoid potholes, debris or parked car doors. Give them room.
Slow down when passing. The rush of air from a fast car can push a bicyclist off balance.
Do not honk close to a bicyclist unless it is needed to prevent a crash. A sudden horn can startle them.
If you cannot pass with enough room, for example on a narrow road with oncoming traffic, slow down, follow at a safe distance and pass only when it is safe.
Do not pass a bicyclist and then turn right in front of them. Slow down, let them go by, and turn behind them.
When turning left, yield to an oncoming bicyclist just as you would to a car. Bikes are often faster than they look.
A bicyclist may use a left-turn lane. If one is ahead of you, stay behind until they finish the turn.
Dim your high beams for an oncoming bicyclist at night.
At night, watch the right edge of the road closely. Bicyclists are hard to see, and some ride without lights.

blocks.text: The minimum distance you must leave when passing a bicyclist varies by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

Bicyclists use hand signals. A left arm bent up at the elbow means a right turn (some riders point the right arm straight out instead). A left arm straight out means a left turn, and a left arm bent down means slowing or stopping.
A motorcycle is entitled to the full width of a lane, the same as a car. Never share a lane with one. To pass a motorcycle, use the next lane as you would to pass a car.

items: The most common car-motorcycle crash is a car turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle.
A motorcycle's small size makes it look farther away and slower than it really is. Take a second look before you turn or pull out.
Many drivers look only for cars and miss motorcycles. Before changing lanes, check your mirrors and turn your head, because a motorcycle can hide in your blind spot.
Motorcycle turn signals often do not cancel by themselves. Wait until you are sure a motorcycle is actually turning before you pull out.
Riders may change speed or position in the lane to avoid gravel, potholes, grates or debris.
Riders often slow by downshifting, which does not light the brake light. Keep a good following distance.
Leave extra following distance behind motorcycles, and even more in rain or darkness.
When a motorcycle passes you, keep your speed and lane position.
At night, a single headlight may be a motorcycle that is closer than it looks. If you are waiting to turn left, let it pass.

sections.heading: Large trucks, buses and light rail

blocks.text: No-Zones are large blind spots in front of, behind and beside a truck or bus where the driver cannot see you. If you cannot see the truck's side mirrors, or the driver's face in them, the driver cannot see you.

items: A loaded truck needs a much longer distance to stop than a car. Never cut in front of one.
Pass on the left side, where the driver can see you better. The right-side No-Zone is especially large.
If you need an exit and a truck is in the right lane just ahead of it, slow down and exit behind the truck.
A truck's size makes it look slower than it really is. Do not underestimate how soon it will reach an intersection.
Trucks and buses make wide right turns and may swing left first, leaving a gap on the right. Never squeeze between a turning truck and the curb, and stop behind the stop line so it has room to turn.
When stopped behind a truck on an uphill, leave extra space. It may roll back when it starts.
Use low beams when following a truck at night. High beams reflect off its big mirrors into the driver's eyes.
When a truck comes toward you on a two-lane road, keep as far right in your lane as is safe. The air blast between you pushes the vehicles apart, so keep a firm grip.
If a truck is backing into a loading dock, wait until it finishes. Do not pass behind it.

blocks.text: Light rail trains and streetcars cannot stop quickly or steer around you. If one is approaching, wait for it to pass before turning across the tracks.

rows: The bus is about to stop. Slow down and get ready to stop.
Flashing red lights and stop arm
Stop and stay stopped until the red lights go off and the bus moves, or the driver or an officer signals you to go.

items: On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions must stop, even if the bus is across the road from you.
Stop whether or not you see children. They can be hidden by the bus.
When the red lights turn off and the bus moves, watch for children and drive slowly past them.
Children are in the most danger when they cross the street after getting off the bus.

blocks.text: Rules for divided highways and how far back you must stop vary by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

Trains always have the right-of-way. A train can take a mile or more to stop and cannot swerve. Because of its size, a train looks farther away and slower than it really is, so never race one to a crossing.

items: At a crossing marked only with a crossbuck, slow down, look both ways, listen, and stop if a train is coming.
Never stop on the tracks. If traffic is backed up past the crossing, wait before the tracks until there is room for your whole car on the other side.
At a crossing with more than one track, wait after a train passes until you can see that no train is coming on any track.
Never drive around or under lowered gates, even if you see no train. If they stay down, call the number on the posted emergency sign.
Stop well back from the tracks, behind any stop line or gate. A train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on each side.
Look and listen at every crossing, every time, even one where you have never seen a train.
Do not follow the car ahead across. Check for trains yourself and make sure there is room.

blocks.text: The exact distance you must stop from the nearest rail varies by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: When an emergency vehicle with a siren or flashing lights approaches, pull to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes.
If you are in an intersection, keep going through it, then pull over. Never stop inside an intersection.
If you hear a siren nearby but cannot tell where it is, pull to the right and stop until you know.
After one passes, check for more before pulling back into traffic. They often travel in groups.
Do not follow closely behind an emergency vehicle using its siren or lights. Stay well back.
Do not drive over a fire hose unless a fire or police official directs you.

blocks.caption: Move Over: change lanes away from a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights if you safely can; if not, slow down.

blocks.text: Every state has a Move Over law, but the details, and how far you must stay behind emergency vehicles, vary. Check your State Cheat Sheet.
In a work zone, flaggers control traffic with STOP/SLOW paddles or red flags. Their directions, like a police officer's, come before normal signs and signals.

rows: Stop and wait until the flagger signals you to go.
Move ahead slowly and carefully, watching for workers.

blocks.caption: An orange triangle with a red border marks a slow-moving vehicle. Slow down.

items: Spot slow-moving vehicles early. At highway speed you close in on them fast and need time to slow down.
Farm equipment may swing left before turning right and may have no turn signals. Hang back until you know what the driver is doing.
Slow-moving vehicles have a right to use the road. Be patient, and pass only where it is legal and you can see it is safe.
Around a person riding a horse, slow down, pass wide and do not honk.
Leave plenty of room behind a horse-drawn vehicle at a stop. It can roll backward.
After passing a horse-drawn vehicle, move back only when you are well ahead of the horse.
If cattle or other animals are near the road, slow down or stop and go on only when it is safe.

keyPoints: Watch for pedestrians near schools, parks and bus stops, and obey school crossing guards.
Bicyclists have the same rights as drivers; pass slowly with plenty of room and never turn right across them.
Motorcycles get a full lane and look farther away than they are; take a second look before turning left.
Stay out of truck No-Zones: if you can't see the driver in the mirror, the driver can't see you.
Stop for a school bus with flashing red lights; on a two-lane road, both directions stop.
Trains always win: never stop on tracks, never go around gates, and look for a second train.
Pull right and stop for emergency vehicles, move over for stopped ones, and obey flaggers.
Slow down early for slow-moving vehicles, horses and livestock, and never honk at horses.
